archetype.name: Gunslinger
archetype.definition: A big-armed, aggressive thrower who keeps challenging tight windows and attacking downfield, accepting interceptions and sacks as the cost of the explosive plays he creates.

report.headline: Same Winston: deep shots pay, intermediate throws bleed, and the sacks pile up.
report.take:
Winston has run the Giants' offense since Week 3, taking over from Jaxson Dart, and he is exactly the quarterback his career says he is. His aggressiveness (20.89% of throws into tight windows) sits right where it was in Tampa, and so does the turnover habit: this is the passer who threw 30 interceptions in 2019 and has ranked near the bottom in bad-throw rate in nearly every charted season. The season line (-0.117 EPA per dropback, 34th of 45; CPOE -8.94, 42nd) looks like a collapse, but much of it comes from the Week 2 relief outing against the Rams (-16.5 EPA, -25.3 CPOE). As a starter he sits at -0.026 EPA per dropback with a -4.8 CPOE. That is below average, not a disaster, and close to his 2021 and 2025 accuracy marks.

The passing game splits cleanly by depth. Throws of 20+ air yards have been his best work at +0.455 EPA, with on-target accuracy for that distance (CPOE -0.4) despite a 34.8% completion rate. Throws of 10-19 yards are where it falls apart: a 46.2% completion rate, -10.3 CPOE and all five of his interceptions. The middle of the field is the same story, with a -16.4 CPOE and three picks. Behind the line of scrimmage, the screens have cost his offense (-0.281 EPA per play), and in shotgun he's at -0.147 per play, while his small under-center sample is slightly positive. That points to a run-leaning Harbaugh offense (pass rate over expected -7.4, 28th) that is more comfortable when it can lean on play-action looks.

The sacks are the other drain. Pressure isn't unusually frequent (19.5% of dropbacks, 17th of 37), but a third of his pressures end in sacks (29th), and his time to throw of 2.64 seconds is not the long hold that usually explains that. On third down, the offense faces an average of 9.7 yards to go and converts only 28.8%, with seven sacks. That is a quarterback and a line losing the down-and-distance battle. The red zone has hidden much of this: six touchdowns on 16 attempts with a +16.5 CPOE. That is a small, hot sample, not a skill he has shown before.

The last three games show the ceiling. He has averaged 242.7 yards and 2.33 touchdowns a game with slightly positive EPA per dropback, and the Washington tie (326 yards, +10.6 EPA) was his best start. But Week 6 against the Saints was a regression to the worst version: -12 EPA, a -15.6 CPOE, two interceptions and only 60% of snaps, which the dossier doesn't explain. He remains QB1 with no injury listed. Expect this to keep swinging week to week, because the profile produces both outcomes.

strengths.title: Real production on deep shots
strengths.body: His 20+ yard throws have produced +0.455 EPA per attempt and are the largest source of value in his season, with near-expected accuracy on difficult throws. That fits a career built on a 10.5-ish aDOT and willingness to push the ball. It is sustainable as a trait, though 23 attempts make the exact rate fragile.

strengths.title: Recent volume and scoring
strengths.body: Over the last three games he has averaged 242.7 passing yards and 2.33 touchdowns, with EPA per dropback back above zero. That makes him a usable producer when the Giants have to throw. It rests partly on soft defenses (Arizona, Washington and New Orleans all rank 26th or worse today), so treat it as his ceiling rather than a new baseline.

strengths.title: Finishing drives in the red zone
strengths.body: Six touchdowns on 16 red-zone attempts at +0.513 EPA has kept his fantasy line afloat despite poor efficiency between the 20s. Winning in tight quarters with Nabers and Likely is plausible, but a +16.5 CPOE on that sample will cool off.

concerns.title: Intermediate and middle-field interceptions
concerns.body: All five interceptions have come on 10-19 yard throws, where he completes under half his passes, and the middle of the field shows a -16.4 CPOE. That is a lifelong pattern, not bad luck: he has ranked in the bottom tier for interceptions and bad throws for most of his career. Expect roughly one pick a game to persist.

concerns.title: Sacks and a weakened line
concerns.body: An 8.7% sack rate (36th) and a 33.3% pressure-to-sack rate stall drives, especially on long third downs. Starting right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (90% of snaps) is out, which removes a regular blocker from a line that already gives up hits. This is part protection, part his habit of holding for the big play, and it likely gets worse before it improves.

concerns.title: Accuracy below league standard
concerns.body: Even setting aside the Week 2 relief outing, his starts carry a -4.8 CPOE, and his 18.4% bad-throw rate ranks 34th of 37. He has never been a precise passer, so this isn't a slump. It is the price of his aggressiveness, and it caps his efficiency in an offense that would rather run.

trend.note: He climbed from a -16.5 EPA relief game through a conservative Titans win to two positive outings against Arizona and Washington. Then he dropped back to -12 EPA against the Saints while playing only 60% of snaps. The swings follow his turnover and sack counts more than his opponents.

nextGame.headline: Safety-depleted, deep-leaky Texans invite shots, but the pass rush looms.
nextGame.body:
Houston's defense is built to stop the run and allow big plays through the air, which matches what Winston does best. The Texans rank 11th against the run and 4th in explosive runs allowed, but 27th in deep-pass EPA and 30th in explosive passes allowed. Offenses pass against them more than usual (a pass funnel, 5th). As 10-point underdogs, the Giants will likely have to throw, which raises his volume. The catch is game script: trailing by nine-plus has been his worst state (-0.189 EPA per play, three interceptions), and Houston's 9th-ranked sack rate meets his biggest weakness.

Availability favors the deep game on both sides. Houston is without safety Jalen Pitre (92% of snaps, out), and fellow safety Reed Blankenship (86%) is questionable after a concussion. That could leave the back end thin against exactly the throws Winston wants to make. On his side, losing right tackle Eluemunor matters against a pass rush that gets home. Mooney (neck, questionable) and Theo Johnson (out) thin the depth behind Nabers and Likely, concentrating targets further. Houston's offense gets Tank Dell back, which could push the Giants into catch-up mode early.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots against a thin secondary
keyMatchups.body: His +0.455 EPA on 20+ yard throws meets a defense ranked 27th in deep-pass EPA, possibly missing both starting safeties. If he gets time, this is where the big plays come from.

keyMatchups.title: Texans' rush against a replacement tackle
keyMatchups.body: Houston sacks quarterbacks on 7.4% of dropbacks (9th), and Winston turns a third of his pressures into sacks. With a starting tackle out, sack-driven drive killers are the main way this game goes wrong.

keyMatchups.title: Nabers against a generous WR1 defense
keyMatchups.body: Opposing WR1s have scored 4.3 PPR points above their averages against Houston (28th), and Nabers leads Winston's targets with positive EPA. The ball should funnel to him.

nextGame.watch: Whether the line holds up long enough for him to attack Houston's depleted safeties deep before the Texans' rush and a big deficit force him into forced intermediate throws.

restOfSeason.body:
The baseline is a volatile, below-average passer whose fantasy value outruns his efficiency. The deep-ball production and aggressiveness are real and career-long. So are roughly one interception a game and a high sack rate, which the injured line won't help. The red-zone touchdown rate is the piece most likely to regress, so expect fewer multi-touchdown games than the last three weeks suggest unless he keeps landing in shootouts. The run-leaning scheme limits his volume when the Giants are competitive. Trailing scripts raise his attempts but also his turnover risk. A fair range is roughly 200-255 passing yards and 1.2-1.9 touchdowns a game, with about one pick.

Job security is a quieter variable. Jaxson Dart started the first two weeks, and Winston played only 60% of snaps in Week 6 for reasons the dossier doesn't give. He is listed QB1, but another game like the Saints loss would invite questions.
swingFactors: Hold on the starting job over Jaxson Dart

confidence.note: Four starts and small splits, but his traits match a long, consistent career.
